title: High-throughput replica-pinning approach to screen for yeast genes controlling low-frequency events
author: Novarina, Rosas Bringas, et al.
materials: 64-bit computer running Linux, Mac OS or Windows
Yeast Knock-Out collection keyfile in 384 format
Note: Instructions about how to install R and R studio, as well as the required R packages can be found in the Readme file of the High-Throughput Replica Pinning script.

steps.title: Prepare non-selective and selective plates
steps.instruction: For each reporter‑containing YKO library plate, prepare at least n non‑selective plates (NSP, YPD) and 2n selective plates (SP, SD‑leu), where n equals the number of replica‑pinning plates used for library amplification. In the example, the 14 YKO plates are replica‑pinned onto 6 NSP plates (n = 6), requiring 14 × 6 = 84 NSP plates and 14 × 6 × 2 = 168 SP plates. Use standard recipes to prepare and sterilize the agar media, pour 40 mL of medium into each PlusPlate on a level surface, and let the plates dry for 2 days at room temperature (20 °C–25 °C). Prepare extra plates as backup, store plates at 4 °C in a sealed plastic bag for up to 3 months, and bring them to the bench a few hours before pinning to allow surface drying.

substeps.instruction: Calculate required NSP and SP plates (NSP = number of library plates × n; SP = NSP × 2).
Prepare agar media (YPD for NSP, SD‑leu for SP) using standard recipes and sterilize.
Pour 40 mL of each medium into each PlusPlate.
Dry plates for 2 days at 20 °C–25 °C.
Optionally prepare additional plates for backup.
Store plates at 4 °C (≤3 months) in a plastic bag; equilibrate on bench before use.

steps.title: Set up data‑analysis environment
steps.instruction: Install R (version 3.6.3 or later) and RStudio, then install the required R packages: tidyverse (1.3.1), optparse (1.6.6) and openxlsx (4.2.4) as listed in the script’s Readme file.

steps.title: Install ImageJ ScreenMill plugin
steps.instruction: Add the ScreenMill Colony Measurement Engine macro to ImageJ.

substeps.instruction: Open ImageJ, choose Plugins → Macro → Install, and select the file “cm engine_ImageJ1.63.txt” from the ImageJ macros folder.
Open the plugin via Plugins → Macro → ScreenMill - CM Engine [c].

steps.title: Measure colony areas on plates
steps.instruction: Quantify colony sizes on non‑selective and selective plates using the ScreenMill plugin.

substeps.instruction: Select Plugins → Macro → ScreenMill - CM Engine, then choose the parent directory containing images of the non‑selective plates.

In the Screen Information menu set: Fine‑crop mode = Automatic; Colony measurement method = Standard; Plate density = 1536; File name for measurements (e.g., “leuDRscreen_NSP_colonyAreas”); Running mode = Standard.
Run the measurement to generate a .txt file of colony areas for NSP plates.
Repeat the same procedure for the selective plates (SP), optionally using the same output folder for both NSP and SP images.

steps.title: Run high‑throughput data analysis script
steps.instruction: Execute the provided R script to calculate SP/NSP colony frequencies and generate a ranked Excel report.

substeps.instruction: Download the High‑Throughput Replica Pinning script from https://github.com/Chang-ERIBA/Protocol_HTRP.
Open a terminal in the directory containing High_Replica_Pinning_Tools.R and High_Replica_Pinning.R.
Run the command: Rscript High_Replica_Pinning.R -i -k -O --Filter --Median_NSP --Median_SP
Provide required input files:
• Colony‑area data file (combined NSP and SP .txt files if processed separately).
• Library keyfile (.csv, 384‑format) with columns Plate #, Row (A‑P), Column (1‑24), ORF, Gene, and optional Mutation.
Optionally specify parameters:
• Output directory (default creates an “Output” folder).
• Minimum total colonies on NSP (default = 10).
• NSP size‑threshold fraction of median colony area (default = 0.5).
• SP size‑threshold fraction of median colony area (default = 0.2).
Run the script; it creates an Excel file named <your‑chosen‑prefix>_…_.xlsx containing tabs: Raw, Raw‑Ordered, Ordered, Ranked, Filtered, and Grouped.

description: This protocol describes a high-throughput replica pinning procedure to screen for genes affecting low-frequency events using an appropriate selectable genetic reporter (Figure 1). We have successfully applied this protocol to study the accumulation of spontaneous mutations during replicative aging using inactivation of the Mother Enrichment Program (Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009) as a readout for spontaneous mutagenesis events (Novarina et al., 2020a), and to screen for genes that affect spontaneous direct-repeat recombination with the leu2ΔEcoRI-URA3-leu2ΔBstEII direct-repeat recombination reporter (Novarina et al., 2020b; Smith and Rothstein, 1999). As a standard example, we describe here the procedure for the spontaneous direct-repeat recombination screen (Novarina et al., 2020b). The protocol can be easily adapted to test other forms of genomic instability, or other low-frequency events, such as gross chromosomal rearrangements (Schmidt et al., 2006), inverted-repeat recombination (Rattray and Symington, 1994), transcription errors (Irvin et al., 2014; Strathern et al., 2012), transient loss of gene silencing (Dodson and Rine, 2015) and read-through at premature termination codons (Altamura et al., 2016), provided a genetically selectable reporter is available or could be developed. A suitable reporter has the following features: (i) it should be possible to select for the presence of the reporter (in the direct-repeat recombination example by selecting for the URA3 marker); (ii) the reporter should allow the positive selection of the desired low-frequency event, based on the ability of cells to grow in selective conditions (in the direct-repeat recombination example, the functional LEU2 gene resulting from spontaneous recombination allows growth on leucine-deprived plates); (iii) the reporter should be compatible with the SGA/SPA procedure (see introducing the reporter in the YKO collection); (iv) the reporter can be based on either auxotrophic or antibiotic-
